title: OPEN Forum, November 2026

cues: press 1: moves to s02 (the first picture, on the dark ground)
note.body:
[The cover; say nothing. It holds through Umair Khan's hand-over while you and Sania walk on. Press when you reach your mark.]
(press)

cues: press 1: the right half arrives, a village of flood-resistant homes of bamboo and lime; the left blurs and dims
press 2: moves to s03
note.body:
[Salaam, and who you are, in your own words. From your notes: "Like many of you in this room, we live between two worlds... But Pakistan has never stopped being part of who we are."]
Sania and I started The Friends of Pakistan to find the people solving Pakistan's biggest problems, and help them grow. It's 2022. Floods we thought we'd see once in a century. Thirty-three million people affected, eight million forced from their homes. And Pakistanis show up, the way we always do. Pakistan is the seventh most generous country on earth; eight in ten of us give. You could feed a family the week after the water comes.
[Say the left half as something you are proud this room did.]
(press)
And the same heart could back the house the next flood can't take. Yasmeen Lari's teams build homes like these from lime, mud and bamboo, with the families who will live in them.
[If you want your own example here, Rizq, from your notes: "How do we make sure this family doesn't go hungry tomorrow?"]
(press)
note.first_line: Sania and I started The Friends of Pakistan to find the people solving Pakistan's biggest problems, and help them grow.

scenes.title: A ward, then a doctor on every screen

cues: press 1: the right half arrives, a woman doctor on a video consultation; the left blurs and dims
press 2: moves to s04
note.body:
It isn't only floods. Every day, families in Pakistan need care they can't reach, and again Pakistanis step up. Indus Hospital and Shaukat Khanum stand because people in rooms like this one gave. You could build a ward, or fill one with beds.
(press)
And the same heart could put to work the women doctors Pakistan trained and then did not use, on a screen, for patients in every district.
[If you prefer your own example: ChildLife Foundation. Checked form: 14 emergency rooms, 300 telemedicine centres, a million teleconsultations.]
(press)
note.first_line: It isn't only floods.

scenes.title: A school, then every public school

cues: press 1: the right half arrives, a government-school teacher with a phone in a full classroom; the left blurs and dims
press 2: moves to s05
note.body:
You could build a school in a village. Children walk through a door that wasn't there before. That's how TCF began: a few schools, and people like you behind them.
(press)
And the same heart could lift what is taught in the tens of thousands of public schools that already stand, where most of Pakistan's children already sit. Haroon will show you what that looks like.
(press)
note.first_line: You could build a school in a village.

scenes.title: A job, then every graduate ready

cues: press 1: the right half arrives, a career session in a public university; the left blurs and dims
press 2: moves to s06
note.body:
You could help one graduate find their first job. That changes a family.
(press)
And the same heart could back the people bringing career guidance into public universities, so whole classes leave ready for work. Amal Academy, one of our Skardu fellows, does exactly that: of their 16,000 graduates, they tell us, eight in ten start meaningful work within three months.
(press)
note.first_line: You could help one graduate find their first job.

cues: press 1: "what" arrives
press 2: "grows." arrives, in green
press 3: moves to s10 (Sania; the ground turns to paper)
note.body:
TCF was a handful of schools once; this room backed it, and it grew. Four times you could do one good thing, and four times the same heart could back the thing that grows. By back, we mean the right blend of capital: a gift, a grant or an investment, whatever helps it grow.
[In your own words: what you and Sania have spent twenty years learning to find. Your countdown line about children dying is left out on purpose: this session asks for no guilt; it is yours to restore. From your notes: "We've seen incredible leaders with solutions that work struggle to raise money."]
(press)
(press)
Back what grows. Sania.
(press)
note.first_line: TCF was a handful of schools once; this room backed it, and it grew.

cues: press 1: the axes and the steady line draw: "One village school."
press 2: the linear line draws, steady cedes: "more schools every year"
press 3: the exponential curve draws, linear cedes: "how every school teaches"; "Back what grows." beneath the chart
press 4: moves to s11
note.body:
Scale is a buzzword, so we have one definition: the sustained acceleration towards the full potential of your idea. Scale has a shape. It's a trajectory, not a number.
(press)
The first shape is steady: a village school, sponsored year after year. It changes that village for good.
(press)
The second is linear: more schools every year. That is how this room built The Citizens Foundation, and the country needed every school. Pakistan's need still grows faster.
(press)
The third is exponential. How every school in the country teaches changes, until the answer overtakes the problem. That's our thesis, in three words.
(press)
note.first_line: Scale is a buzzword, so we have one definition: the sustained acceleration towards the full potential of your idea.

scenes.title: Who does it, and who pays

cues: press 1: the two cards: "The government takes it into its budget." · "Or others copy the model."
press 2: the cards cede; the two lines draw: the budget levels off, the impact climbs
press 3: moves to s12
note.body:
An organisation with exponential ambition knows it can't do it alone. So it asks two questions early: who delivers this at scale, and who pays for it at scale?
(press)
There are two answers. Either the government takes it on and puts it in its budget, or other organisations copy the model and run it.
(press)
When one of those answers exists, the organisation's budget levels off while the impact goes through the roof. A dollar in, exponential impact out.
(press)
note.first_line: An organisation with exponential ambition knows it can't do it alone.

cues: press 1: "All foreign aid, one year: $4.6 billion"
press 2: "Foreign investment, one year: $1.6 billion"
press 3: "The IMF programme, three years: $7 billion"
press 4: moves to s13
note.body:
Here is what Pakistanis abroad send home every year: more than forty billion dollars, a record. Most of it is wages sent to family, and it should be. That green bar is the river.
(press)
All the foreign aid Pakistan receives in a year: four and a half billion. The river is ten times that.
(press)
All the foreign investment in a year: one and a half billion.
(press)
And the IMF programme the whole country argues about: seven billion, over three years. Pakistanis abroad send that home every two months.
(press)
note.first_line: Here is what Pakistanis abroad send home every year: more than forty billion dollars, a record.

cues: press 1: the bar ("What goes home.") divides into slices: a family, a school, a ward, relief; "A portfolio."
press 2: the thin slice at the end lights green: "what grows"
press 3: moves to s14
note.body:
Every dollar of that river is love for someone. A family's fees. A school in the village your parents left. A bed in a ward. Relief after the water comes. Keep all of it.
(press)
Think of your giving as a portfolio. Every slice stays.
(press)
The question is only this: what portion of it backs what grows? When a dollar backs something exponential, it goes much further.
(press)
note.first_line: Every dollar of that river is love for someone.

cues: press 1: the second card, Ireland; India cedes
press 2: moves to s15
note.body:
Other communities like ours did this on purpose. Two-thirds of the investment that opened China came from Chinese abroad. Indian-Americans give four to five billion dollars a year, and Pratham, built with it, reaches seven million children.
(press)
One Irish-American put 1.6 billion euros into Ireland's universities, and the state matched it many times over. None of them stopped giving to family. They added something that grew.
(press)
note.first_line: Other communities like ours did this on purpose.

cues: press 1: three fellows step forward, one line each
press 2: "Find. Refine. Fund."
press 3: moves to s16
note.body:
This is the next generation: ten founders Nadir and I met in Skardu in June, on their way to scale.
(press)
As they told us: a help-line that has supported 25,000 people; a divorce file from a lawyer who fought 160 of these cases; a programme that protects eight in ten children exposed to TB.
(press)
Our whole job is finding them, and bringing them to you. Find. Refine. Fund.
(press)
note.first_line: This is the next generation: ten founders Nadir and I met in Skardu in June, on their way to scale.

scenes.title: This is what it looks like

cues: press 1: "This is what it looks like."
press 2: moves to s20, Haroon's cover
note.body:
Back what grows. I want to prove it to you.
(press)
Taleemabad is on a mission to make sure every kid reaches grade-level literacy and numeracy. They're rapidly scaling across Pakistan's public school system, and doing so well that about a year ago, education organisations all over the world started clamouring for access to the open-source tools they'd built. So today we can confidently say Taleemabad is not just scaling in Pakistan but exporting its genius internationally as well. Here is what backing what grows looks like. Haroon.
(press)
note.first_line: Back what grows.

I'd seen the magic, and I couldn't unsee it. Then I saw the size of it: fifty-eight million children in school.

note.first_line: I'd seen the magic, and I couldn't unsee it.

(press)
[Let the map land.]
(press)
More than eight million children a week.

We were recognised at Buckingham Palace. But who were we kidding? Ten minutes a day was never going to change a child's life.

So we went back to schools: the low-fee private schools families pay for.
(press)
We have a Harvard in Pakistan at five dollars a month. And a rundown Stanford, only a dollar more.
(press)
We gave them our name, lessons and training. In the first year, two hundred schools carried our name.
[Only if ahead of the clock. In your own words, if you want it: "as far as we could tell, the fastest-growing chain in the country".]
(press)
note.first_line: So we went back to schools: the low-fee private schools families pay for.

This time we measured, every term, against the school next door. Next door, forty-one in a hundred children read at grade level. In ours, sixty-four.
(press)
Half as many again. They were finally reading close to grade level.
(press)
note.first_line: This time we measured, every term, against the school next door.

press 4: moves to s41
note.body:
[Presenter clock: about 4:00 here, the room's applause and laughter included. If you are past 4:30, take the shortest line on every scene from here.]
When something is this cheap and this effective, do you know what happens?
(press)
The state comes calling.
[Pause for the laugh. The smile is at ourselves.]
We doubted them. We said: a whole district, and you pay. They said yes.
(press)
Four thousand teachers in 422 schools, at eight dollars a child.
[Only if ahead of the clock. In your own words, if you want them: the 136,000 children and the two million dollars are yours to say; neither is on screen.]
(press)
More than half of Pakistan's schoolchildren are in public schools. We changed to meet them.
(press)
note.first_line: When something is this cheap and this effective, do you know what happens?

In 2023, as AI arrived, we built on WhatsApp: every teacher we met had it, even near retirement. Today's lesson plan, in Urdu, English or Sindhi. They record the class, and a voice note comes back. Listen.
(press)
[Let it play.] Some teachers started telling it about their hard days.
(press)
A quiz goes home to the parent's phone.
[Press once more: the quiz says well done, 3 s. Let it finish.]
And the exams mark themselves.
(press)
note.first_line: In 2023, as AI arrived, we built on WhatsApp: every teacher we met had it, even near retirement.

Pakistan is four countries stitched together. We handed the government our brand, and word travelled.
(press)
Islamabad, where the government pays for every school.
(press)
Balochistan.
(press)
Punjab.

And Sindh, where we are starting, and where we've found some of the warmest welcomes.

(press)
note.first_line: Pakistan is four countries stitched together.

And we open-sourced all of it.

Tanzania first.

And our biggest deployment outside Pakistan: three thousand teachers in Palestine so far, five thousand under contract.
[In your own words, a breath: what it means to you that this was built in Pakistan. Anything about what the West Bank has lived this year is yours to say or leave.]
(press)
Teams in India and Niger have taken the code themselves. Pakistan is now exporting education.
(press)
note.first_line: Then other countries found it.

When the cheapest way to teach a child to read is Pakistani and open source, every government comes.
